o: A linear selection requires consecutive picked indices j and j' to satisfy prices[j'] - prices[j] == j' - j, i.e. prices[j] - j is constant along the whole selection. So valid selections live entirely inside a group of days sharing the same value of prices[i] - i. Since all prices are positive, the best selection in a group takes every element of it; the answer is the maximum group sum. Example 1: group d=3 gives {5,7,8} sum 20; example 2: d=4 gives everything, sum 35.
k: The linearity condition means prices[i] - i is invariant across the selection.
Group indices by prices[i] - i with a hash map; any subset of a group is a valid linear selection.
Prices are positive, so taking an entire group is always at least as good as a subset.

a.i: Bucket each element under key prices[i] - i and accumulate sums; the answer is the largest bucket sum. Correctness follows because within a bucket every pair satisfies the difference condition, and mixing buckets breaks it.
s: Initialize a map from difference d = prices[i] - i to accumulated sum.
Scan once, adding prices[i] into bucket prices[i] - i.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) average map operations.
a.sp: O(n) — up to n distinct buckets.

w: Watch for overflow: sums reach 1e5 * 1e9 = 1e14, so use 64-bit integers in C++/Java. A common pitfall is using 0-indexed differences inconsistently — any consistent shift works since only equality matters. Follow-up: what if prices could be negative? Then you'd take only positive-prefix subsets within each group.
